Coherence from Randomness:
Sub-keV Dark Matter Scattering off Random, Heterogeneous Materials

Zhi-Han Liu Affiliation: College of Science, China University of Petroleum (East China), Qingdao 266580, China    Shigeki Matsumoto Email: shigeki.matsumoto@ipmu.jp Affiliation: Kavli IPMU (WPI), UTIAS, University of Tokyo, Kashiwa, 277-8583, Japan    Jie Sheng Email: jie.sheng@ipmu.jp Affiliation: Kavli IPMU (WPI), UTIAS, University of Tokyo, Kashiwa, 277-8583, Japan    Chuan-Yang Xing Email: cyxing@upc.edu.cn Affiliation: College of Science, China University of Petroleum (East China), Qingdao 266580, China
Abstract

The sub-keV mass range has long posed a challenge for the direct detection of dark matter via elastic scattering. In this Letter, we propose a new mechanism in which dark matter, assumed to be quadratically coupled to SM particles, scatters from random heterogeneous materials with intrinsic density fluctuations, yielding an enhanced coherent response. This effect can substantially increase the total scattering rate and induce measurable accelerations of the target. Using this idea, we derive new constraints from the MICROSCOPE mission that extend into previously unexplored parameter space for sub-keV dark matter, probing cross sections down to ∼4×10−38​cm2\sim 4\times 10^{-38}\,\mathrm{cm^{2}}.

I Introduction

Dark matter (DM), accounting for ∼85%\sim 85\% of the matter content of the Universe [10], remains one of the most profound mysteries in modern physics, with its fundamental properties still largely unknown [18, 19, 16]. Among the various strategies proposed to unveil its interactions with the Standard Model (SM), direct detection experiments play a central role [51, 20]. In particular, elastic scattering between DM and SM particles provides a theoretically well-motivated and experimentally accessible avenue, and constitutes the primary target signal in many ongoing and forthcoming direct-detection searches [61, 6, 4, 12, 21, 1, 14, 9].

Direct detection is further enriched by the phenomenon of coherent enhancement [34, 11, 52, 8, 35], which can substantially and significantly amplify the scattering rate when the DM de Broglie wavelength, λχ≃|𝐪|−1\lambda_{\chi}\simeq|{\bf q}|^{-1}, exceeds the characteristic size of the target. Here, |𝐪||{\bf q}| denotes the momentum transfer. In this regime, the scattering amplitudes from individual constituents add constructively, yielding a total cross section that remarkably scales with the square of the number of scatterers [37, 30, 44]. A well-known example occurs for weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) heavier than the GeV scale: because their de Broglie wavelength exceeds the nuclear radius, they scatter coherently off all nucleons in the nucleus, resulting in an A2A^{2} enhancement, where AA is the atomic mass number [44]. Analogous coherence effects for MeV-scale DM interacting with the collective electron cloud have likewise been explored to boost the scattering rate [38].

The role of coherence becomes even more striking for ultralight bosonic DM that is quadratically coupled to SM fields [34, 8, 26, 45, 36, 47, 5]. In such scenarios, the de Broglie wavelength can easily exceed macroscopic scales, for example, meV-scale DM has λχ\lambda_{\chi} of order meters, allowing it to scatter coherently off an entire bulk target. This macroscopic coherence leads to an enormous enhancement of the total scattering cross section proportional to Ntot2N_{\mathrm{tot}}^{2}, where Ntot∼1023N_{\mathrm{tot}}\sim 10^{23} denotes the total number of nucleons in a laboratory-scale detector [26, 45, 47]. Despite this dramatic amplification, the energy transferred in a single scattering event is exceedingly small, typically Δ​E≲10−5​eV\Delta E\lesssim 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{eV}, rendering calorimetric detection infeasible. Importantly, while the energy transfer is suppressed by the large target mass, the momentum transfer is not; the cumulative impulse from the high event rate can therefore induce a tiny but potentially measurable acceleration of the target [26, 45, 47]. This observation motivates force- or acceleration-based search strategies, such as asymmetric precision torsion-balance experiments, exploiting macroscopic coherence to probe quadratically coupled DM in the sub-eV mass regime [45, 47].

As the DM mass increases, its de Broglie wavelength becomes shorter than the detector size RR, and macroscopic coherence is lost, since scattering amplitudes from distant regions acquire varying phases and interfere destructively. For a spherical, homogeneous target, the resulting form-factor suppression scales as (|𝐪|​R)−4(|{\bf q}|\,R)^{-4} [8, 47], so the effective cross section decreases rapidly as the momentum transfer, thus the DM mass, grows. In the sub-keV range, the coherence length reaches only micrometer scales, far smaller than typical force sensors, and the energy deposited in scattering, Δ​E∼10−3​eV\Delta E\sim 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{eV}, is still below calorimetric thresholds [32, 31, 25, 33, 40, 41]. This combination of suppressed coherence and tiny energy deposition makes this sub-keV mass regime difficult to probe with existing direct-detection methods [15, 25, 41].

In this work, we show that the loss of macroscopic coherence at sub-keV masses does not prevent significant enhancement: even when the DM wavelength λχ\lambda_{\chi} is much smaller than the detector size, coherent scattering can still occur locally if the target is a random, heterogeneous material. Such materials contain many micron-scale patches with different densities or compositions, and when the patch size ξ\xi is comparable to the DM wavelength, ξ∼|𝐪|−1\xi\sim|{\bf q}|^{-1}, DM scatters coherently within each patch, while contributions from distant patches add only incoherently. With a nucleon density of the detector n0∼Ntot/R3n_{0}\sim N_{\rm tot}/R^{3}, the total cross section scales as σtot∝[Ntot/(n0​ξ3)]​(n0​ξ3)2∼Ntot​n0​ξ3∼Ntot2​(|𝐪|​R)−3\sigma_{\rm tot}\propto[N_{\rm tot}/(n_{0}\xi^{3})](n_{0}\xi^{3})^{2}\sim N_{\rm tot}\,n_{0}\,\xi^{3}\sim N_{\rm tot}^{2}(|{\bf q}|R)^{-3}, giving a parametric enhancement over the homogeneous case. Using a general formalism to quantify this effect, we show that heterogeneous materials can substantially boost the scattering rate of quadratically coupled DM with sub-keV masses. Applying the framework to the MICROSCOPE test masses, we obtain direct-detection bounds on the DM–nucleon cross section as strong as 10−38​cm210^{-38}\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}, and argue that future torsion-balance experiments using materials with larger density contrasts could improve the sensitivity by additional orders of magnitude, potentially reaching scattering cross sections of order 10−42​cm210^{-42}\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}.

II Coherence in Randomness

Considering a quadratic coupling between DM and nucleons, such as an interaction of the form (mN/Λ2)​χ2​N¯​N(m_{N}/\Lambda^{2})\chi^{2}\bar{N}N for scalar11 1 In the mass range below ∼0.2​keV\sim 0.2\,\mathrm{keV}, DM must be bosonic due to the so-called Tremaine–Gunn bound [56, 29, 13], whereas in the mass interval of 0.2​–​1​keV0.2\text{--}1\,\mathrm{keV} DM can be either bosonic or fermionic. DM χ\chi, where N=n,pN=n,p denotes neutrons or protons, the DM can scatter off terrestrial targets. In the sub-keV mass regime, the DM de Broglie wavelength (mχ​vχ)−1(m_{\chi}v_{\chi})^{-1}, with a typical velocity of the DM vχ∼10−3v_{\chi}\sim 10^{-3} in the laboratory frame, exceeds the micron scale and is much larger than the interatomic spacing of order 10−10​m10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}. Therefore, one can adopt a mean-field description of the target, in which the discrete atomic structure is replaced by a smooth number-density profile n⁡(𝐫)n(\mathbf{r}).

Given the weakness of the DM interaction, the Born approximation can be employed. The differential scattered wave from all nucleons within a volume element,

d​Ψsc​(𝐫)=f⁡(θ)​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫1​ei​k​|𝐫||𝐫|​n​(𝐫1)​d3​𝐫1,d\Psi_{\rm sc}(\mathbf{r})=f(\theta)\,e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{1}}\,\frac{e^{ik|{\bf r}|}}{|{\bf r}|}\,n(\mathbf{r}_{1})\,d^{3}\mathbf{r}_{1}, (1)

is obtained by summing the single-nucleon amplitudes f⁡(θ)f(\theta), each weighted by the phase factor 𝐪⋅𝐫1\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{1} with 𝐪=𝐤−𝐤′\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{k}^{\prime}, assuming a spin-independent interaction between the DM and a nucleon. Here, θ\theta is the scattering angle, and k=|𝐤|=|𝐤′|k=|\mathbf{k}|=|\mathbf{k}^{\prime}| denotes the DM wavenumber. Since the DM is much lighter than the nucleons, the magnitudes of the initial and final momenta, 𝐤\mathbf{k} and 𝐤′\mathbf{k}^{\prime}, remain essentially unchanged during scattering. Integrating over the entire target and squaring the resulting amplitude gives the total differential cross section.

d​σtotd​Ω=d​σχ​Nd​Ω​∫d3​𝐫1​d3​𝐫2​ei​𝐪⋅(𝐫2−𝐫1)​n​(𝐫1)​n​(𝐫2),\frac{d\sigma_{\rm tot}}{d\Omega}=\frac{d\sigma_{\chi N}}{d\Omega}\int d^{3}\mathbf{r}_{1}d^{3}\mathbf{r}_{2}\;e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_{2}-\mathbf{r}_{1})}\,n(\mathbf{r}_{1})\,n(\mathbf{r}_{2}), (2)

where d​σχ​N/d​Ω=|f⁡(θ)|2d\sigma_{\chi N}/d\Omega=|f(\theta)|^{2} is the differential cross section for scattering between the DM particle and a nucleon.

For a homogeneous target of volume VV with constant density n⁡(𝐫)=n0n(\mathbf{r})=n_{0}, the double integral in Eq. (2) depends only on the target geometry and overall size. With the total number of scatterers given by Ntot=n0​VN_{\mathrm{tot}}=n_{0}V, the differential cross section can then be factorized as

d​σtotd​Ω=Ntot2​|Fhomo​(𝐪)|2​d​σχ​Nd​Ω,\frac{d\sigma_{\rm tot}}{d\Omega}=N_{\mathrm{tot}}^{2}\,|F_{\rm homo}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}\,\frac{d\sigma_{\chi N}}{d\Omega}, (3)

with the dimensionless form factor defined as

|Fhomo​(𝐪)|2≡n02Ntot2​∫d3​𝐫1​d3​𝐫2​ei​𝐪⋅(𝐫2−𝐫1).|F_{\rm homo}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}\equiv\frac{n_{0}^{2}}{N_{\mathrm{tot}}^{2}}\int d^{3}\mathbf{r}_{1}d^{3}\mathbf{r}_{2}\;e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_{2}-\mathbf{r}_{1})}. (4)

If the separation |𝐫2−𝐫1||{\bf r}_{2}-{\bf r}_{1}|, which is typically of the order of the target size, is much smaller than the DM wavelength, |𝐫2−𝐫1|≪q−1≡|𝐪|−1|{\bf r}_{2}-{\bf r}_{1}|\ll q^{-1}\equiv|\mathbf{q}|^{-1}, then |Fhomo|≃1|F_{\rm homo}|\simeq 1, i.e., the scattering is coherent across the entire target, yielding an Ntot 2N_{\mathrm{tot}}^{\,2} enhancement relative to the single-nucleon scattering cross section. Conversely, when the wavelength becomes shorter, the phase oscillates rapidly, the integral is suppressed, and coherence is consequently lost.

For a homogeneous sphere of radius RR, the form factor can be analytically evaluated in the following form:

|Fhomo​(𝐪)|2=[3​(sin⁡(q​R)−q​R​cos⁡(q​R))(q​R)3]2,|F_{\rm homo}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}=\left[\frac{3\big(\sin(qR)-qR\cos(qR)\big)}{(qR)^{3}}\right]^{2}, (5)

whose envelope scales as (q​R)−4(qR)^{-4} at large q​RqR. Denoting Nc≡(4​π/3)​λχ3​n0N_{c}\equiv(4\pi/3)\,\lambda_{\chi}^{3}n_{0} as the number of scatterers within one DM wavelength, the total cross section scaling for DM scattering off a homogeneous target can be written as σtot∝Ntot2​|Fhomo|2∝R6×(λχ4/R4)∝Ntot2/3​Nc4/3\sigma_{\rm tot}\propto N_{\rm tot}^{2}|F_{\rm homo}|^{2}\propto R^{6}\times(\lambda_{\chi}^{4}/R^{4})\propto N_{\rm tot}^{2/3}N_{c}^{4/3}, where we have used the relation Ntot⁡(c)∝R3​(λχ3)N_{\rm tot(c)}\propto R^{3}(\lambda_{\chi}^{3}). This scaling drops rapidly as the DM wavelength becomes shorter.

We now arrive at the key point of our work: the total scattering cross section of sub-keV DM can be greatly enhanced when the target is a random heterogeneous material. In a random medium, the exact density function is not known deterministically and can be defined as

n⁡(𝐫)≡n0+δ​n​(𝐫),n(\mathbf{r})\equiv n_{0}+\delta n(\mathbf{r}), (6)

with n0≡⟨n⁡(𝐫)⟩n_{0}\equiv\langle n(\mathbf{r})\rangle being the average density and δ​n\delta n the corresponding density fluctuation, satisfying ⟨δ​n​(𝐫)⟩=0\langle\delta n(\mathbf{r})\rangle=0. Here ⟨⋯⟩\langle\cdots\rangle denotes an ensemble average. The properties of a random material are largely encoded in its two-point correlation function ⟨n⁡(𝐫1)​n​(𝐫2)⟩\langle n(\mathbf{r}_{1})\,n(\mathbf{r}_{2})\rangle, which measures how the density at 𝐫2\mathbf{r}_{2} co-varies with that at 𝐫1\mathbf{r}_{1} in space. A large value of ⟨n⁡(𝐫1)​n​(𝐫2)⟩\langle n(\mathbf{r}_{1})\,n(\mathbf{r}_{2})\rangle indicates that the material tends to exhibit similar densities at the two points. According to Eq. (6), this correlation naturally splits as

⟨n⁡(𝐫1)​n​(𝐫2)⟩=n02+⟨δ​n​(𝐫1)​δ​n​(𝐫2)⟩.\langle n(\mathbf{r}_{1})n(\mathbf{r}_{2})\rangle=n_{0}^{2}+\langle\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{1})\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{2})\rangle. (7)

The first term corresponds to the contribution from the homogeneous average density, while the second term encodes the resulting effect of local fluctuations.

Similarly, the total scattering cross section for DM interacting with a target composed of a random material should also be obtained by averaging Eq. (2), yielding

⟨d​σtotd​Ω⟩=Ntot2​|F⁡(𝐪)|2​d​σχ​Nd​Ω.\left\langle\frac{d\sigma_{\rm tot}}{d\Omega}\right\rangle=N_{\mathrm{tot}}^{2}\,|F(\mathbf{q})|^{2}\,\frac{d\sigma_{\chi N}}{d\Omega}. (8)

As indicated in Eq. (7), the form factor in this case

|F⁡(𝐪)|2≡|Fhomo​(𝐪)|2+|Ffluc​(𝐪)|2,|F(\mathbf{q})|^{2}\equiv|F_{\rm homo}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}+|F_{\rm fluc}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}, (9)

receives contributions both from the form factor of a homogeneous medium, as in Eq. (4), and from the effects of density fluctuations that arise in random materials,

|Ffluc​(𝐪)|2≡1Ntot2​∫d3​𝐫1​d3​𝐫2​ei​𝐪⋅(𝐫2−𝐫1)​⟨δ​n​(𝐫1)​δ​n​(𝐫2)⟩,|F_{\mathrm{fluc}}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}\equiv\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{tot}}^{2}}\int d^{3}\mathbf{r}_{1}d^{3}\mathbf{r}_{2}\;e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_{2}-\mathbf{r}_{1})}\,\langle\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{1})\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{2})\rangle, (10)

which captures the distinctive scattering properties of random heterogeneous media in a consistent manner.

Random heterogeneous materials typically exhibit clustering, in which atoms aggregate into groups whose characteristic size ξ\xi sets the scale over which the density field is correlated. At coincident points (𝐫1=𝐫2\mathbf{r}_{1}=\mathbf{r}_{2}), the correlation of the density fluctuation δ​n\delta n is maximal, with ⟨δ​n2​(𝐫)⟩=δ​n2¯\langle\delta n^{2}(\mathbf{r})\rangle=\overline{\delta n^{2}} defining the variance. For separations satisfying |𝐫2−𝐫1|≪ξ|\mathbf{r}_{2}-\mathbf{r}_{1}|\ll\xi, the fluctuations δ​n​(𝐫1)\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{1}) and δ​n​(𝐫2)\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{2}) take similar values, yielding a large correlation ⟨δ​n​(𝐫1)​δ​n​(𝐫2)⟩\langle\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{1})\,\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{2})\rangle. In contrast, when |𝐫2−𝐫1|≫ξ|\mathbf{r}_{2}-\mathbf{r}_{1}|\gg\xi, the fluctuations become statistically independent and ⟨δ​n​(𝐫1)​δ​n​(𝐫2)⟩≈⟨δ​n​(𝐫1)⟩​⟨δ​n​(𝐫2)⟩=0\langle\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{1})\,\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{2})\rangle\approx\langle\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{1})\rangle\,\langle\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{2})\rangle=0. This behavior typically reflects a generic property of random media: correlations are strong at short distances and decay to zero at long distances, with the length scale ξ\xi characterizing this decay referred to as the correlation length.

A two-phase system whose components have random shapes and sizes is often called a Debye random medium [28, 27]. Its correlation function ⟨δ​n​(𝐫1)​δ​n​(𝐫2)⟩\langle\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{1})\,\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{2})\rangle is closely approximated by an exponential form [43],

⟨δn(𝐫1)δn(𝐫2)⟩=δ​n2¯e−|𝐫2−𝐫1|/ξ\langle\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{1})\,\delta n(\mathbf{r}_{2})\rangle=\overline{\delta n^{2}}\,e^{-|\mathbf{r}_{2}-\mathbf{r}_{1}|/\xi} (11)

with a strong short-distance correlation that decreases and approaches zero at sufficiently large separations.

The fluctuation-induced form factor of a spherical target with radius RR can be obtained by inserting Eq. (11) into Eq. (10) and then simply taking the limit R≫ξR\gg\xi,

|Ffluc​(𝐪)|2=δ​n2¯n02​6​ξ3R3​(1+q2​ξ2)2.|F_{\mathrm{fluc}}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}=\frac{\overline{\delta n^{2}}}{n_{0}^{2}}\,\frac{6\,\xi^{3}}{R^{3}\big(1+q^{2}\xi^{2}\big)^{2}}. (12)

For ξ≃q−1∼λχ\xi\simeq q^{-1}\sim\lambda_{\chi}, this fluctuation-induced form factor scales as ξ3/R3∼(q​R)−3\xi^{3}/R^{3}\sim(qR)^{-3}. For materials with large density contrast, δ​n2¯≃n02\overline{\delta n^{2}}\simeq n_{0}^{2}, and recalling that |Fhomo​(𝐪)|2∝(q​R)−4|F_{\mathrm{homo}}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}\propto(qR)^{-4}, the fluctuation form factor dominates in the regime q−1≪Rq^{-1}\ll R, i.e., |Ffluc​(𝐪)|2≫|Fhomo​(𝐪)|2|F_{\mathrm{fluc}}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}\gg|F_{\mathrm{homo}}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}, so that |F⁡(𝐪)|2≈|Ffluc​(𝐪)|2|F(\mathbf{q})|^{2}\approx|F_{\mathrm{fluc}}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}. This implies that the total cross section scales as σtot∝Ntot2​|Ffluc​(𝐪)|2∝Ntot​Nc\sigma_{\rm tot}\propto N_{\mathrm{tot}}^{2}\,|F_{\mathrm{fluc}}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}\propto N_{\mathrm{tot}}\,N_{c}, where Nc≡(4​π/3)​λχ3​n0∼(4​π/3)​ξ3​n0N_{c}\equiv(4\pi/3)\,\lambda_{\chi}^{3}n_{0}\sim(4\pi/3)\,\xi^{3}n_{0}. Thus, the total scattering cross section of sub-keV DM can receive a substantial enhancement by a factor of (Ntot/Nc)1/3∼(R/ξ)(N_{\mathrm{tot}}/N_{c})^{1/3}\sim(R/\xi) compared to the case of a homogeneous material.

This realizes the intuitive picture emphasized in the Introduction: DM scatters coherently within each cluster, whereas the contributions from distinct clusters add incoherently, as illustrated clearly in Fig. 1. At fixed qq, the form factor in Eq. (12) is maximized at ξ=3/q\xi=\sqrt{3}/q, which reflects the optimal balance between the cluster size and the onset of significant phase decorrelation.

For short-wavelength DM, the form factor |F⁡(𝐪)|2|F(\mathbf{q})|^{2} shows very little dependence on the overall target geometry. Physically, the DM “sees” the medium only over clusters of size ξ≃q−1\xi\simeq q^{-1}, and amplitudes from different clusters add incoherently. Consequently, the result is governed primarily by the underlying fluctuation statistics rather than by how clusters are assembled into macroscopic targets. This geometry insensitivity is confirmed numerically. As shown in Fig. 2, at q=0.1​eVq=0.1\,\mathrm{eV} the form factors for spherical and cubic targets with the same volume V=1​cm3V=1\,\mathrm{cm^{3}} are nearly indistinguishable.

III Acceleration from DM Scattering

Due to the rotation of the Solar System around the Galactic Center, there exists a relative velocity between the Solar System and the dark-matter (DM) halo, typically |𝐯χ|≃10−3|\mathbf{v}_{\chi}|\simeq 10^{-3} in the laboratory frame. With such a velocity, the energy transferred in sub-keV DM scattering lies far below the thresholds of conventional direct-detection experiments. However, light DM has a high number density, nχ≡ρχ/mχn_{\chi}\equiv\rho_{\chi}/m_{\chi}, where ρχ≃0.4​GeV/cm3\rho_{\chi}\simeq 0.4~\mathrm{GeV/cm}^{3} is the local DM density, and its scattering cross section with a macroscopic target can be coherently enhanced, yielding a sizable overall scattering rate. Continuous DM scattering can thus induce a measurable acceleration of the target, providing a unique observable for probing light DM [26, 45, 47]. Averaging over the DM phase space, the DM-induced acceleration of the target along the detection axis (taken to be the zz-axis) is given by [45, 47]

az=nχmtot​∫d3​𝐯χ​𝑑Ω​qz​|𝐯χ|​f​(𝐯χ)​⟨d​σtotd​Ω⟩.a_{z}=\frac{n_{\chi}}{m_{\mathrm{tot}}}\int d^{3}\mathbf{v}_{\chi}\,d\Omega\,q_{z}\,|\mathbf{v}_{\chi}|\,f(\mathbf{v}_{\chi})\,\left\langle\frac{d\sigma_{\rm tot}}{d\Omega}\right\rangle. (13)

Here, mtotm_{\mathrm{tot}} is the total target mass, f⁡(𝐯χ)f(\mathbf{v}_{\chi}) is the DM velocity distribution in the laboratory frame [17], and qzq_{z} is the zz-component of the momentum transfer 𝐪\mathbf{q}.

The observable scales as a∼σtot/mtota\sim\sigma_{\text{tot}}/m_{\text{tot}}, where the total target mass is proportional to the number of atoms, mtot∝Ntotm_{\text{tot}}\propto N_{\mathrm{tot}}. For sub-keV DM scattering off a random material, the total cross section behaves as σtot∝Nc​Ntot\sigma_{\text{tot}}\propto N_{c}N_{\mathrm{tot}}, so the factor of NtotN_{\mathrm{tot}} cancels, yielding an additional enhancement by NcN_{c} in the induced acceleration. Such accelerations can be sensitively probed in equivalence-principle tests, including the MICROSCOPE satellite mission [54, 55] and torsion-balance experiments.

IV Implementation in MICROSCOPE

The MICROSCOPE space mission was designed to test the weak equivalence principle (EP) by precisely monitoring the differential acceleration of two concentric cylindrical test masses in low-Earth orbit [54, 55]. These test masses are made of two distinct materials, a Pt–Rh alloy and a Ti–6Al–4V alloy (90% Ti, 6% Al, 4% V). The latter is a random two-phase alloy in which the α\alpha phase (hexagonal close-packed (HCP), Al-enriched) and the β\beta phase (body-centered cubic (BCC), V-enriched) coexist with different densities and compositions [42].

When sub-keV DM flows through the apparatus, it scatters off both test masses. The coherent enhancement of scattering on the uniform Pt–Rh alloy is suppressed compared to that on the Ti–6Al–4V alloy because of its random two-phase structure. As indicated by Eq. (13), this difference in the total cross sections of the two test masses induces a measurable differential acceleration.

Since the exact microstructure of the Ti–6Al–4V alloy used in the MICROSCOPE experiment is not publicly available, we adopt as a benchmark the sample characterized in Ref. [42], whose lattice parameters and phase densities are summarized in Table 1. Together with the reported phase fractions, fα=74.39%f_{\alpha}=74.39\% and fβ=25.61%f_{\beta}=25.61\% [42], one can compute the average nucleon density and the variance of its density fluctuations as

n0=2.69×1024/cm3,δ​n2¯=(7.29×1022/cm3)2.n_{0}=2.69\times 10^{24}/\mathrm{cm^{3}},~~\overline{\delta n^{2}}=\left(7.29\times 10^{22}/\mathrm{cm^{3}}\right)^{2}. (14)

The detailed procedure for computing the density and its fluctuations from the material information is given in Appendix A. In addition, the two-point correlation function of the Ti–6Al–4V alloy was measured experimentally in Ref. [46]. The reported correlation function is well described by the simple exponential form in Eq. (11), with a characteristic correlation length ξ\xi of about 2​μ​m2\,\mu\mathrm{m}.

The MICROSCOPE test bodies are cylindrical shells whose size is much larger than the correlation length ξ\xi, so the form factor is essentially insensitive to their global geometry. We therefore approximate them as solid spheres with the same mass in our analysis and employ Eq. (12) to evaluate the fluctuation-induced form factor.

The DM-induced acceleration can be obtained by integrating Eq. (13) under the assumption of an isotropic differential cross section, d​σχ​N/d​Ω=σχ​N/4​πd\sigma_{\chi N}/d\Omega=\sigma_{\chi N}/4\pi. Due to the self-rotation of the MICROSCOPE satellite with frequency fs=2.94×10−3​Hzf_{s}=2.94\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Hz} [54], the DM-induced acceleration is modulated at a frequency fDM=fsf_{\rm DM}=f_{s}. This is close to the frequency of the equivalence-principle (EP)-violating signal induced by the Earth’s gravity, fEP=fo+fs=3.11×10−3​Hzf_{\rm EP}=f_{o}+f_{s}=3.11\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Hz}, where fo=1.68×10−4​Hzf_{o}=1.68\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Hz} is the orbital frequency of the satellite [54]. Therefore, the constraints reported for EP violation, Δ​a≲4.8×10−14​m​s−2\Delta a\lesssim 4.8\times 10^{-14}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}} at 95% C.L. [55], can be used as a benchmark for DM-induced acceleration. We find that the MICROSCOPE mission is sensitive to σχ​N\sigma_{\chi N} as small as 4×10−38​cm24\times 10^{-38}\,\mathrm{cm^{2}} around mχ≃0.02​keVm_{\chi}\simeq 0.02\,\mathrm{keV}, with the sensitivity gradually decreasing toward higher mχm_{\chi}, as shown in Fig. 3.

V Torsion Balance Experiment

Torsion-balance (TB) experiments provide the highest sensitivity to differential accelerations between test bodies, reaching sensitivities of order 10−15​m/s210^{-15}\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}} [50, 58, 62]. However, test bodies in torsion-balance experiments are typically fabricated from compositionally homogeneous materials such as high-purity metals [49, 22, 7, 53, 50, 58] or quartz crystals [62]. Such choices preclude taking advantage of the coherence enhancement we propose for random heterogeneous media and are therefore not optimal for efficiently probing light sub-keV DM scattering.

In future TB experiments, employing random heterogeneous materials with large density contrasts as test bodies can improve sensitivity to sub-keV DM scattering. One practical way to realize large density fluctuations with a controllable correlation length is to use commercially available porous tungsten. Porous tungsten, resembling a sponge with internal voids, is produced by pressing high-purity tungsten powder followed by high-temperature sintering. The correlation length can be tuned by varying the grain size of the precursor powder, while the number-density variance reaches its maximum when the pore volume fraction is around 50%50\%, yielding

δ​n2¯=n02=(5.80×1024​cm−3)2.\overline{\delta n^{2}}=n_{0}^{2}=\left(5.80\times 10^{24}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\right)^{2}. (15)

This variance is about four orders of magnitude larger than that of the Ti-6Al-4V alloy shown in Eq. (14).

When future TB experiments with test bodies of correlation length ξ=2​μ​m\xi=2\,\mathrm{\mu m}, as in MICROSCOPE, achieve an acceleration sensitivity of Δ​a∼10−15​m​s−2\Delta a\sim 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}} [50, 58, 62], which is about one order of magnitude stronger than MICROSCOPE, the sensitivity to the DM–nucleon cross section could improve by around five orders of magnitude. This would correspond to a projected limit of

σχ​N≲5×10−43​cm2.\sigma_{\chi N}\lesssim 5\times 10^{-43}\,\mathrm{cm^{2}}. (16)

This projection is shown as the dashed curve in Fig. 3.

VI Other Constraints

Although sub-keV DM carries too little kinetic energy to be detected in conventional direct-detection experiments, it can be boosted by cosmic rays to relativistic speeds, enabling elastic scattering off liquid-xenon targets and depositing recoil energies above threshold. Such cosmic-ray–boosted DM is constrained by PandaX-II [24], CDEX-10 [60], LZ [2], and Super-Kamiokande [3]. These limits are largely insensitive to the DM mass for two reasons: at smaller mass the DM number density is higher, while the energy transferred in each scattering is correspondingly smaller [59].

In addition to direct detection, light DM is also constrained by astrophysical observations. The basic idea is that DM can be produced in stellar interiors through nucleon bremsstrahlung [48], Compton scattering [48], or electron–ion bremsstrahlung [39], thereby carrying away energy and modifying stellar cooling. The most stringent bounds arise from supernova cooling. However, in supernova cores the nucleon density is so high that DM with sufficiently strong interactions becomes trapped and cannot escape, causing the supernova limits to saturate at large cross sections. On the other hand, strong interactions are constrained by horizontal branch (HB) stars, where DM emission mainly originates from electron–ion bremsstrahlung [39], as shown by the light gray region in Fig. 3. The evaluation of these stellar-cooling constraints is detailed in Appendix B. Our mechanism is capable of probing the currently unconstrained region between the supernova limits and the HB-star constraints.

VII Conclusion

The coherence effect can substantially enhance the scattering cross section of light DM on macroscopic targets. In this Letter, we demonstrate that random materials with small-scale density fluctuations exhibit an enhanced coherent response to sub-keV DM scattering, thereby amplifying the accelerations induced in the target by the continuous DM flux. We develop a general theoretical framework based on density–density correlation functions to compute the scattering form factor of random media. Within this framework, the MICROSCOPE experiment sets stringent constraints on sub-keV DM that surpass those from cosmic-ray–boosted DM and HB-star cooling, reaching σχ​N≃10−38​cm2\sigma_{\chi N}\simeq 10^{-38}\,\mathrm{cm}^{2} for mχ≃10​eVm_{\chi}\simeq 10\,\mathrm{eV}. Future torsion-balance experiments employing optimized random materials could further improve the sensitivity, allowing this new mechanism to probe regions of parameter space that were previously inaccessible.

Appendix A Density Variance of Ti-6Al-4V Alloy

The microstructure of the Ti-6Al-4V alloy under various heat-treatment conditions has been investigated in Ref. [42]. As a representative example throughout this work, we consider the benchmark sample “HT850WC+AG”, in which the alloy is heat-treated at 850∘850^{\circ}C for 2 hours, followed by water quenching and subsequent aging (reheating) at 500∘500^{\circ}C for 3 hours. The weight fractions of (Ti, Al, V) in the α\alpha phase are measured to be (92.05%, 6.30%, 1.66%), while those in the β\beta phase are (88.44%, 5.50%, 6.05%). In addition, the α\alpha phase has a hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure with lattice parameters aα=2.9228​Åa_{\alpha}=2.9228\,\text{\AA} and cα=4.6692​Åc_{\alpha}=4.6692\,\text{\AA}, whereas the β\beta phase has a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure with lattice parameter aβ=3.2001​Åa_{\beta}=3.2001\,\text{\AA}. The volumes of their primitive cells can be calculated as

Vcell,α\displaystyle V_{\mathrm{cell},\alpha} =32​aα2​cα=34.54​Å3,\displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a_{\alpha}^{2}c_{\alpha}=34.54\,\text{\AA}^{3}, (17a)
Vcell,β\displaystyle V_{\mathrm{cell},\beta} =aβ3=32.77​Å3.\displaystyle=a_{\beta}^{3}=32.77\,\text{\AA}^{3}. (17b)

Using the atomic weights of (mTi,mAl,mV)=(47.867,26.982,50.942)(m_{\mathrm{Ti}},m_{\mathrm{Al}},m_{\mathrm{V}})=(47.867,26.982,50.942) in atomic mass units, one can calculate the densities of the two phases as follows:

ρ=NcellVcell​(fN,Ti​mTi+fN,Al​mAl+fN,V​mV).\rho=\frac{N_{\mathrm{cell}}}{V_{\mathrm{cell}}}(f_{N,\mathrm{Ti}}\,m_{\mathrm{Ti}}+f_{N,\mathrm{Al}}\,m_{\mathrm{Al}}+f_{N,\mathrm{V}}\,m_{\mathrm{V}}). (18)

Here, NcellN_{\mathrm{cell}} denotes the number of atoms in the primitive unit cell. For both the two phases α\alpha and β\beta, these are

Ncell,α=Ncell,β=2.N_{\mathrm{cell},\alpha}=N_{\mathrm{cell},\beta}=2. (19)

The volume of the primitive unit cell, VcellV_{\mathrm{cell}}, is given in Eq. (17). Here, fN,if_{N,i} denotes the number fraction of element ii in the phase. It can be obtained from the weight fractions fw,if_{w,i} in each phase measured in Ref. [42]. The mass of species ii in the material is Mi=fw,i​MM_{i}=f_{w,i}M, and the corresponding number of atoms is Ni=fw,i​M/miN_{i}=f_{w,i}M/m_{i}. The number fraction fN,if_{N,i} is defined as the ratio of NiN_{i} to the total number of atoms, so that the total mass MM simply cancels. Consequently, the resulting relation between the number fractions fN,if_{N,i} and the weight fractions fw,if_{w,i} is

fN,i=fw,i/mifw,Ti/mTi+fw,Al/mAl+fw,V/mV.f_{N,i}=\frac{f_{w,i}/m_{i}}{f_{w,\mathrm{Ti}}/m_{\mathrm{Ti}}+f_{w,\mathrm{Al}}/m_{\mathrm{Al}}+f_{w,\mathrm{V}}/m_{\mathrm{V}}}. (20)

Substituting Eq. (20) into Eq. (18), the density becomes

ρ=NcellVcell​1fw,Ti/mTi+fw,Al/mAl+fw,V/mV.\rho=\frac{N_{\mathrm{cell}}}{V_{\mathrm{cell}}}\frac{1}{f_{w,\mathrm{Ti}}/m_{\mathrm{Ti}}+f_{w,\mathrm{Al}}/m_{\mathrm{Al}}+f_{w,\mathrm{V}}/m_{\mathrm{V}}}. (21)

Using the measured parameters listed above, the densities of the α\alpha and β\beta phases are explicitly obtained as

ρα\displaystyle\rho_{\alpha} =4.39​g/cm3,\displaystyle=4.39\,\mathrm{g/cm^{3}}, (22a)
ρβ\displaystyle\rho_{\beta} =4.66​g/cm3.\displaystyle=4.66\,\mathrm{g/cm^{3}}. (22b)

Because the primitive cell of the α\alpha phase has a larger volume and contains a higher proportion of aluminum atoms, the density is lower than that of the β\beta phase.

The volume fractions of the α\alpha and β\beta phases in the alloy are measured to be 74.39%74.39\% and 25.61%25.61\%, respectively [42]. The resulting average density of the alloy is given by

ρ¯=0.7439​ρα+0.2561​ρβ=4.46​g/cm3,\bar{\rho}=0.7439\,\rho_{\alpha}+0.2561\,\rho_{\beta}=4.46\,\mathrm{g/cm^{3}}, (23)

which is consistent with the density of the Ti-6Al-4V alloy, 4.42​g/cm34.42\,\mathrm{g/cm^{3}}, used in the MICROSCOPE mission [54]. Correspondingly, the nucleon number densities in the α\alpha and β\beta phases are then given approximately by

nα\displaystyle n_{\alpha} =2.65⋅1024​cm−3,\displaystyle=2.65\cdot 10^{24}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}, (24a)
nβ\displaystyle n_{\beta} =2.81⋅1024​cm−3.\displaystyle=2.81\cdot 10^{24}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}. (24b)

The average nucleon number density in the alloy is,

n¯=0.7439​nα+0.2561​nβ=2.688⋅1024​cm−3,\bar{n}=0.7439\,n_{\alpha}+0.2561\,n_{\beta}=2.688\cdot 10^{24}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}, (25)

while the variance of the number density is

δ​n2¯=0.7439​(nα−n¯)2+0.2561​(nβ−n¯)2=(7.29⋅1022​cm−3)2.\begin{split}\overline{\delta n^{2}}&=0.7439(n_{\alpha}-\bar{n})^{2}+0.2561(n_{\beta}-\bar{n})^{2}\\ &=\left(7.29\cdot 10^{22}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\right)^{2}.\end{split} (26)

All relevant parameters of the two phases are summarized in Tab. 1 in the main text for easy reference.

Appendix B Astrophysical Constraints

The constraints from stellar cooling relevant to this work arise from supernovae and horizontal-branch stars.

Supernova – Light DM that couples to nucleons can be produced in the core of supernovae via nucleon bremsstrahlung, thereby affecting the cooling process. However, if the interaction strength is sufficiently large, the produced DM particles become trapped within the core and can no longer efficiently transport energy away. In this trapping regime, the DM particles can be treated as blackbody radiation emitted from a DM-sphere inside the core. Inside the DM-sphere, the DM remains in thermal equilibrium with the surrounding medium, while outside it the DM free-streams out of the core. Then, the corresponding DM luminosity is given by [48, 23],

Lχ=gχ​π120​4​π​rsp2​Tsp4,L_{\chi}=\frac{g_{\chi}\pi}{120}4\pi r_{\mathrm{sp}}^{2}T_{\mathrm{sp}}^{4}, (27)

where gχg_{\chi} is the number of degrees of freedom of the DM particle, and rspr_{\mathrm{sp}} and TspT_{\mathrm{sp}} denote the characteristic radius and temperature of the DM-sphere, respectively.

The radius of the DM-sphere is set by requiring that a DM particle undergo approximately one scattering while traveling from the DM-sphere to the core edge,

∫rsp∞d​rλχ≃1,\int_{r_{\mathrm{sp}}}^{\infty}\frac{dr}{\lambda_{\chi}}\simeq 1, (28)

where the DM mean free path in the core is given by

λχ≡mNρ​σχ​N,\lambda_{\chi}\equiv\frac{m_{N}}{\rho\,\sigma_{\chi N}}, (29)

where mNm_{N} is the nucleon mass, ρ\rho is the mass density of nucleons in the core, and σχ​N\sigma_{\chi N} is the DM scattering cross section with nucleons. The density profile of the core can be approximated by a power-law function as [57, 48]

ρ⁡(r)=ρR​(Rr)γ,\rho(r)=\rho_{R}\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^{\gamma}, (30)

where ρR≃1014​g/cm3\rho_{R}\simeq 10^{14}\,\mathrm{g/cm^{3}} is the density at R≃10​kmR\simeq 10\,\mathrm{km}, and the power-law index γ\gamma typically lies in the range 33–77. For a constant cross section σχ​N\sigma_{\chi N}, integrating Eq. (28) gives

σχ​N​ρR​RγmN​rsp1−γγ−1≃1.\sigma_{\chi N}\frac{\rho_{R}R^{\gamma}}{m_{N}}\frac{r_{\mathrm{sp}}^{1-\gamma}}{\gamma-1}\simeq 1. (31)

The maximal scattering cross section for DM to escape from the DM-sphere can be analytically obtained as

σχ​N≃(γ−1)​mN​rspγ−1ρR​Rγ.\sigma_{\chi N}\simeq\frac{(\gamma-1)m_{N}r_{\mathrm{sp}}^{\gamma-1}}{\rho_{R}R^{\gamma}}. (32)

The luminosity of new particles emitted from the supernova is constrained to be Lχ≲2×1052​erg/sL_{\chi}\lesssim 2\times 10^{52}\,\mathrm{erg/s} [23]. Using this constraint, together with the local radial temperature profile of the protoneutron star reported in Ref. [23], we determine, in our benchmark scenario, the corresponding DM-sphere radius and temperature to be rsp≃19​kmr_{\mathrm{sp}}\simeq 19\,\mathrm{km} and Tsp≃7.5​MeVT_{\mathrm{sp}}\simeq 7.5\,\mathrm{MeV}, respectively. This, in turn, yields a robust upper limit on the cross section,

σχ​N≃4.7×10−42​cm2,\sigma_{\chi N}\simeq 4.7\times 10^{-42}\,\mathrm{cm^{2}}, (33)

taking γ=7\gamma=7 as a benchmark. Dark matter with a cross section larger than this value is trapped in the core and is therefore not constrained by supernova cooling.

Horizontal-Branch (HB) Stars – Dedicated studies of HB-star cooling constraints on quadratically coupled light dark matter are not available. Nevertheless, for linearly coupled scalar particles ϕ\phi with interaction g​ϕ​N¯​Ng\phi\bar{N}N, the cooling effects have been extensively studied in detail [39]; the production of ϕ\phi is dominated by electron–ion bremsstrahlung in HB stars, and the upper bound on the coupling is g2/4​π≃5×10−23g^{2}/4\pi\simeq 5\times 10^{-23} for mϕ≲10​keVm_{\phi}\lesssim 10\,\mathrm{keV} [39]. We translate this bound into the corresponding constraint on the quadratically coupled light dark matter χ\chi considered here by comparing their production rates in HB stars.

The thermal energy in HB stars is of order 10​keV10\,\mathrm{keV}, which is much larger than the DM mass but much smaller than both electron and nucleon masses. Consequently, the emitted DM particles can be treated as relativistic, whereas the electrons and nucleons participating in the scattering process are nonrelativistic. In this regime, the matrix element for single-ϕ\phi bremsstrahlung emission can be approximated as ℳϕ≃(i​g/ωk)​ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{\phi}\simeq(ig/\omega_{k})\,\mathcal{M}_{0}, where ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} is the amplitude for the underlying electron or nucleon interaction without final-state emission, and ωk\omega_{k} is the energy of the emitted ϕ\phi with four-momentum k≃(ωk,𝐤)k\simeq(\omega_{k},{\bf k}). The prefactor i​g/ωkig/\omega_{k} arises from the fermion propagator. This approximation is valid as long as ωk≪mN\omega_{k}\ll m_{N}. When the scalar ϕ\phi is soft, the nucleon propagator is almost on-shell and the cross section of ϕ\phi-emission can be factorized as

d​σϕ≈d​σ0×g2ωk2​d3​𝐤(2​π)3​2​ωk,d\sigma_{\phi}\approx d\sigma_{0}\times\frac{g^{2}}{\omega_{k}^{2}}\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{3}2\omega_{k}}, (34)

where d​σ0d\sigma_{0} is the cross section of electron-ion interaction without the final state emission. The energy-loss rate in HB stars is proportional to the thermal average ⟨ωk​σ​vrel⟩\langle\omega_{k}\,\sigma\,v_{\rm rel}\rangle. For single-scalar emission, it is given by

⟨ωk​σϕ​vrel⟩\displaystyle\langle\omega_{k}\sigma_{\phi}v_{\mathrm{rel}}\rangle ≃σ0​vrel×∫g2ωk2​ωk​d3​𝐤(2​π)3​2​ωk\displaystyle\simeq\sigma_{0}v_{\mathrm{rel}}\times\int\frac{g^{2}}{\omega_{k}^{2}}\omega_{k}\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{3}2\omega_{k}} (35)
=σ0​vrel×g22​π2​Emax,\displaystyle=\sigma_{0}v_{\mathrm{rel}}\times\frac{g^{2}}{2\pi^{2}}E_{\max},

where EmaxE_{\max} denotes the maximum energy of the emitted ϕ\phi, which is of order 10​keV10\,\mathrm{keV} in typical HB stars.

Now, we compute the energy-emission rate of quadratically coupled DM χ\chi with interaction χ2​N¯​N/fN\chi^{2}\bar{N}N/f_{N} in HB stars, and derive the corresponding constraint by relating it to that of the scalar field ϕ\phi; under similar assumptions as before, the cross section can be approximated as,

d​σ2​χ≈d​σ0​1fN2​(ωk1+ωk2)2​d3​𝐤1(2​π)3​2​ωk1​d3​𝐤2(2​π)3​2​ωk2.d\sigma_{2\chi}\approx d\sigma_{0}\frac{1}{f_{N}^{2}(\omega_{k_{1}}+\omega_{k_{2}})^{2}}\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{k}_{1}}{(2\pi)^{3}2\omega_{k_{1}}}\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{k}_{2}}{(2\pi)^{3}2\omega_{k_{2}}}. (36)

Compared with Eq. (34), the only difference is that the final state now contains two DM particles with momenta k1k_{1} and k2k_{2}, so the momentum flowing through the fermion propagator becomes (k1+k2)(k_{1}+k_{2}). The corresponding energy-emission rate in HB stars is then given as follows:

⟨(ωk1+ωk2)​σ2​ϕ​vrel⟩≃σ0​vrel×ℐ,\langle(\omega_{k_{1}}+\omega_{k_{2}})\sigma_{2\phi}v_{\mathrm{rel}}\rangle\simeq\sigma_{0}v_{\mathrm{rel}}\times\mathcal{I}, (37)

where the integration represented by ℐ\mathcal{I} is defined as,

ℐ\displaystyle\mathcal{I} ≡∫1fN2​(ωk1+ωk2)2​(ωk1+ωk2)​d3​𝐤1(2​π)3​ 2​ωk1​d3​𝐤2(2​π)3​ 2​ωk2\displaystyle\equiv\int\frac{1}{f_{N}^{2}(\omega_{k_{1}}+\omega_{k_{2}})^{2}}(\omega_{k_{1}}+\omega_{k_{2}})\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{k}_{1}}{(2\pi)^{3}\,2\omega_{k_{1}}}\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{k}_{2}}{(2\pi)^{3}\,2\omega_{k_{2}}}
=116​π4​fN2​∫∫ω1​ω2ω1+ω2​d​ω1​d​ω2=Emax3288​π4​fN2.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{16\pi^{4}f_{N}^{2}}\int\int\frac{\omega_{1}\omega_{2}}{\omega_{1}+\omega_{2}}\,d\omega_{1}d\omega_{2}=\frac{E_{\max}^{3}}{288\pi^{4}f_{N}^{2}}. (38)

The maximum energy released is still Emax∼T∼10​keVE_{\max}\sim T\sim 10\,\mathrm{keV} in HB stars, set by the temperature. The ratio of the energy-emission rates in the ϕ\phi and χ\chi scenarios is

ΓϕΓ2​χ∼g2​Emax/(2​π2)Emax3/(288​π4​fN2)=144​π2​g2​fN2Emax2.\frac{\Gamma_{\phi}}{\Gamma_{2\chi}}\sim\frac{g^{2}E_{\max}/(2\pi^{2})}{E_{\max}^{3}/(288\pi^{4}f_{N}^{2})}=\frac{144\pi^{2}g^{2}f_{N}^{2}}{E_{\max}^{2}}. (39)

The HB constraint on the ϕ\phi coupling is g2/(4​π)<5×10−23g^{2}/(4\pi)<5\times 10^{-23}; this can be translated into a constraint on fNf_{N} as

1fN2<4​π​144​π2Emax2​5×10−23≈1(10.6​TeV)2​(10​keVEmax)2.\frac{1}{f_{N}^{2}}<4\pi\frac{144\pi^{2}}{E_{\max}^{2}}5\times 10^{-23}\approx\frac{1}{(10.6\,\mathrm{TeV})^{2}}\left(\frac{10\,\mathrm{keV}}{E_{\max}}\right)^{2}. (40)

Therefore, the corresponding bound on the scattering cross section between χ\chi and a nucleon NN is given by

σχ​N=14​π​fN2≃2.77×10−37​cm2​(10​keVEmax)2.\sigma_{\chi N}=\frac{1}{4\pi f_{N}^{2}}\simeq 2.77\times 10^{-37}\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}\left(\frac{10\,\mathrm{keV}}{E_{\max}}\right)^{2}. (41)
